gotcha_text: Landlords use relocation clauses to move profitable salons to inferior, low-visibility units to accommodate higher-rent tenants. This maneuver often leaves the salon owner burdened with the massive costs of moving specialized plumbing and electrical infrastructure.

deep_dive_html:
The Perils of Unregulated Relocation

The relocation clause is one of the most predatory provisions in a commercial lease, particularly for salon operators. While landlords argue these clauses are necessary for center-wide re-tenanting strategies, the practical application often results in the forced migration of a tenant from a high-traffic, anchor-adjacent position to a 'dead' corner or a space with insufficient utility capacity. For a salon, the danger is not merely the change in physical location, but the potential destruction of specialized capital improvements.

A landlord's right to relocate, if left unmitigated, allows them to move you to a space that lacks the necessary drainage for wash stations or the voltage required for professional-grade dryers. This effectively forces the tenant to fund a new, expensive build-out under duress, essentially subsidizing the landlord's desire to reconfigure the property. Furthermore, if the new space lacks the same visibility or foot traffic, the salon's revenue will plummet while the tenant's fixed overhead remains unchanged.

Securing Salon-Specific Protections

To protect your enterprise, you must move beyond simple 'comparable space' language. A sophisticated tenant demands a 'Relocation Standard' that includes several non-negotiable pillars of protection. Market-standard protection requires that any relocated space must be of equal or greater utility, visibility, and foot traffic, and that the landlord bears the entirety of the financial burden associated with the transition.

  • Infrastructure Parity: The new space must possess identical or superior plumbing, electrical, and HVAC capabilities to your current unit.
  • Landlord-Funded Build-Out: The landlord must be contractually obligated to pay 100% of all costs associated with the move, including demolition, installation, and permit fees.
  • Visibility and Traffic Guarantees: The new unit must have equivalent frontage, signage visibility, and foot traffic metrics.
  • Right of Refusal: The tenant must have the absolute right to reject any space that does not meet the predefined criteria.
  • Business Interruption Indemnity: The landlord must compensate the tenant for lost revenue during the period of downtime required for the move.
